.pdim-scratch-external_maxcore-989/exter.module_purpose: A NumPy-based emulation layer for CUDA's execution model (the 'digital GPU'). It supplies dim3, shared memory, warp shuffle/reduce, atomics, math and fp16 intrinsics, and a per-block CUDARuntime context. A launch_kernel helper loops over the grid and calls one vectorised Python kernel function per block. SM102 kernel implementations are written against it. The module docstring states it is not a CUDA interpreter.

symbols.invariants: __slots__ restricts attributes to x, y, z. No validation that values are positive ints.

symbols.intent: Perform one butterfly reduction step of a warp reduction. Each lane adds the value from lane+offset, and lanes with no source keep their own value.

symbols.intent: Emulate a CUDA <<<grid, block>>> launch by looping over every block index (z, y, x order) and calling the Python kernel once per block with a fresh CUDARuntime.
symbols.inputs: kernel_fn(rt, *args), grid and block (Dim3, int or tuple), shared_n_floats, and *args forwarded to the kernel.
symbols.outputs: None. Kernels communicate results through their array arguments.
symbols.side_effects: Runs the kernel function, which typically mutates the argument arrays. Constructs a new CUDARuntime per block.
symbols.invariants: Blocks run sequentially. thread_idx is always (0,0,0), because kernels are vectorised across threads. Each block gets fresh shared memory.
symbols.evidence: L235-259; the docstring says 'single Python call per block is exact'. Called by CUDAModule.__call__ and the native_simt demo tools.

open_questions: The module docstring says atomicAdd is 'numpy += under a threading.Lock', but atomic_add takes no lock, and _AtomicFloat and CUDARuntime._atomics are unused. Is multi-threaded block execution planned?
WarpState.shfl_down_sync fuses the shuffle with an add, which deviates from real CUDA semantics. This looks intentional for reduction use, but the name is misleading.
The listed callers for many symbols are name collisions with unrelated code, so true usage of utilities such as Dim3.volume, SharedMemory.nbytes and the math intrinsics is unknown.

Concrete backends (digital, GPU, cluster, ASIC) subclass it so the runtime can dispatch IR ops interchangeably.

.task123-publishing-candidate/.pdim-clus.module_purpose: This is an esbuild-bundled ESM file, `cluster-fixture.mjs`, that sits in a temporary PDIM cluster-test directory. It inlines much of the Max Booster server: log sanitization, a PDIM/Redis-compatible client with circuit breaker and adaptive queueing, compression engines such as xz/zstd/brotli, container and pocket codecs, worker/compute sizing, the local PDIM store with persistence and Pub/Sub streaming, and PDIM recovery and snapshot authority logic. Only a few excerpts are visible. Entries with no visible body are inferred from names only, with low confidence. The 'callers' lists in the inventory point to unrelated Python files and are name collisions, so they say nothing about how these JS functions are actually used.

symbols.intent: esbuild helper that wraps a module initializer in a lazy, run-once function (`__init`). The result is cached, and a thrown error is remembered and rethrown on later calls.
symbols.inputs: fn: object whose first own property is the module body; res and err are internal cache slots.
symbols.outputs: A function (`__init`) that runs the body once and returns its result.
symbols.side_effects: Runs the module body on the first call and clears `fn`.
symbols.invariants: The body runs at most once. A failure is sticky.
symbols.evidence: cluster-fixture.mjs L3-10; the `init_XzEngine = __esm({...})` pattern.

symbols.intent: The inner lazy initializer returned by `__esm`. It executes the wrapped module body once, caches the result, and rethrows a cached error on later calls.
symbols.outputs: The cached result of the module body.
symbols.side_effects: Runs the wrapped init code. Sets `err` on failure.
symbols.invariants: Idempotent. A failure is never retried.

symbols.intent: esbuild helper that defines enumerable getter properties on a target so a bundled module's namespace exports stay live bindings.
symbols.inputs: target object; `all` is a map of name to getter.
symbols.invariants: Properties are enumerable and getter-only.

symbols.outputs: Sanitized string, with matches replaced by the REDACTED constant. Only valid IPs, as checked by `isIP`, are redacted.
symbols.invariants: Regexes are applied in sequence. Key=value redaction keeps the key prefix via `$1`.
symbols.evidence: L18-23; imports `isIP` from node:net.

symbols.intent: Recursively produce a log-safe copy of an arbitrary value. Strings are sanitized, sensitive keys are redacted, and Errors are flattened. Cycles, depth, array length and key count are bounded.
symbols.inputs: value: any; seen: WeakSet; depth: number.
symbols.outputs: Sanitized primitive, array, or null-prototype object. Placeholders are '[Circular]', '[LOG_DEPTH_LIMIT]', '[BINARY]', '[ACCESSOR]' and '[LOG_ITEM_LIMIT]'.
symbols.side_effects: None. It does not invoke getters and drops prototype-pollution keys.
symbols.invariants: Depth is at most 12. At most 100 items or keys are kept. Keys matching `sensitiveKey` have their values redacted. `seen` is cleaned in `finally`, so only true cycles are flagged.

symbols.side_effects: Spawns a child process. Swallows stdin EPIPE errors.

symbols.evidence: L2765-2788; used by XzEngine.compress/decompress.

symbols.intent: Read and trim a cgroup limit file. Returns null if it is missing (ENOENT/ENOTDIR) and rethrows other errors.
symbols.invariants: Absence is tolerated. Other IO errors propagate.

symbols.intent: Compute the container-aware CPU count and memory in GiB. It takes the minimum of the OS-reported values and the cgroup v2/v1 limits.
symbols.invariants: Never exceeds host values. Limits that are not positive or not finite are ignored.

symbols.intent: Read a numeric env var, falling back to a default, and require it to be a positive finite number. Otherwise it throws.
symbols.invariants: The result is greater than 0 and finite.

symbols.intent: Decide how many cluster workers to run and how much memory and heap each gets. It uses cgroup-aware capacity, reserves headroom, primary, sidecar and python memory, and splits the remainder between app workers and MaxCore workers (70/30 when MAXCORE_LOCAL is on). It honors an env override and a maxWorkers cap, and throws if the budget is insufficient.
symbols.inputs: opts {envOverrideVar, memPerWorkerGB, maxWorkers}; many env vars.
symbols.outputs: Sizing object: workerCount, source (auto/capped/override), workerMemoryMB, workerHeapMB, primaryHeapMB, cpuLimit, memLimit, reservationsMB, and more.
symbols.side_effects: Reads env and cgroup files. Throws on an invalid configuration.
symbols.invariants: The override must be an integer between 1 and min(cpuLimit, memLimit, maxWorkers). Headroom is below 100%. Worker CPU share is at most 1. Heap is 60% of the worker RSS allocation. The inventory's 'stub=empty' flag is wrong, since a full body is present.
symbols.evidence: L2845 onward, excerpt shows full body.

symbols.intent: Build the loopback exec URL of the local in-process PDIM server.
symbols.invariants: Always binds to 127.0.0.1.

symbols.intent: Check that this process has a listening local PDIM HTTP server bound to 127.0.0.1:LOCAL_PORT.

symbols.intent: Guard that the configured PDIM exec backend is this process's owned local store before a snapshot is taken. Throws if the URL is invalid, the server is not listening on loopback, the port, origin or path differ, or the source path is not the expected persistence file.
symbols.invariants: All conditions must match exactly. Paths are compared after resolution.

symbols.intent: Produce a pinned, consistent read-only handle on the local PDIM persistence file for recovery or backup. It verifies authority, synchronously commits the store, checks the file is a regular non-symlink, opens an fd, and verifies the inode is stable.

.task123-publishing-candidate/.pdim-scra.module_purpose: A pure-Python/NumPy emulation substrate for CUDA's execution model, used by the SM102 kernel implementations on the 'digital GPU'. It provides dim3, per-block shared memory, warp shuffle/reduction primitives, atomics, math and half-precision intrinsics, a per-block CUDARuntime context, and a sequential launch_kernel loop over the grid. It is explicitly not a CUDA interpreter. Kernels are Python functions that are vectorised over threads and called once per block (module docstring, launch_kernel docstring).

symbols.intent: Read the JSON body of a batch API response and validate it strictly against the ids that were requested. It throws on any inconsistency and otherwise returns a typed BatchResult.
symbols.inputs: response: a fetch Response whose body is JSON; expectedIds: string[] of ids sent in the request.
symbols.outputs: Promise<BatchResult> with success, failed, the totals, and optional downloadUrl, exportId and comparisonData. Rejects with an Error on invalid shape, count mismatch, or ids that were not requested.
symbols.side_effects: Consumes the response body via response.json(), which can itself throw on malformed JSON. Otherwise pure.
symbols.invariants: success and failed must be arrays of strings and {id, error} objects. totalRequested must equal expectedIds.length, totalSucceeded must equal success.length, and totalFailed must equal failed.length. success plus failed must cover exactly the requested count. Every returned id must be in the requested set. downloadUrl may be string, null or undefined; exportId must be a string if present; comparisonData must be an array if present. Duplicate ids are not detected, so success and failed could overlap or repeat while still satisfying the count checks.
symbols.evidence: File L88-151. The inventory's 'stub=None' agrees; the body is fully implemented. It is called by useBatchAction.execute.

symbols.intent: Core hook that runs one batch operation against the generic batch endpoint. It tracks status (idle, confirming, processing, completed, partial, failed, cancelled), progress, result and error. It shows toasts, invalidates React Query keys on completion, and offers confirm, cancel, reset and retryFailed controls.
symbols.inputs: options: { onSuccess, onError, onProgress, simulateProgress (default true) }. execute takes a BatchActionConfig { resource, action, ids, data, messages, invalidateQueries }.
symbols.outputs: UseBatchActionReturn: status, progress, result, error, execute, confirm, cancel, reset, retryFailed, isProcessing, isComplete, pendingConfig.
symbols.side_effects: Sends an API request via apiRequest (PUT for update, POST otherwise). Starts and stops a 200ms setInterval for fake progress. Shows toasts, calls the onSuccess/onError/onProgress callbacks, and invalidates queries via queryClient. Updates several pieces of React state.
symbols.invariants:
Endpoint is `/api/batch/${resource}/${suffix}` and the body is {ids, data}. Status is 'completed' when there are no failures, 'partial' when some succeeded, and 'failed' when all failed. onSuccess fires for completed and partial but not for all-failed. On exception the error is rethrown after setting state. Simulated progress is capped at total-1 until the response arrives.

Known flaws:
- The AbortController is created but its signal is never passed to apiRequest, so cancel() does not abort the request. The request can still finish and overwrite the 'cancelled' status.
- execute clears pendingConfig on success and never sets it. retryFailed requires pendingConfig, so it returns null after a normal execute and only works if pendingConfig is somehow set again.
- confirm() only stores the config and sets status to 'confirming'. Nothing runs it automatically; the caller must invoke execute(pendingConfig).
- No unmount cleanup for the interval, and a second concurrent execute would orphan the previous interval.
symbols.missing: Pass abortController.signal to the request and handle abort. Keep the last config so retryFailed works after execute. Add interval cleanup on unmount and a guard against overlapping executes.
symbols.evidence: File L153-388. The inventory marks it 'stub=empty', but the body is fully implemented. The abort controller is used only in cancel/finally (L255, L300ff). retryFailed reads pendingConfig, while execute calls setPendingConfig(null).

symbols.intent: Parse and strictly validate the JSON body of a batch-action HTTP response into a BatchResult. It rejects any payload that is inconsistent with the IDs that were requested.
symbols.inputs: response: fetch Response whose body is JSON; expectedIds: string[] that were submitted
symbols.outputs: Promise<BatchResult> with success, failed, totals and optional downloadUrl, exportId, comparisonData and jobId. Throws Error('Batch operation returned an invalid response') or Error('...results for unexpected items') on bad data.
symbols.side_effects: Consumes the response body via response.json(). No other I/O.
symbols.invariants: Requires success to be a string array and failed to be {id, error} objects. totalRequested must equal expectedIds.length, totalSucceeded must equal success.length, and totalFailed must equal failed.length. success.length + failed.length must equal expectedIds.length. Every returned ID must be in the requested set. Optional string fields must be string or null/undefined, and comparisonData must be an array if present.
symbols.evidence: useBatchActions.execute calls it at the `await parseBatchActionsResponse(response, ids)` line. The explicit validation chain is in L110-173. It does not check for duplicate IDs across success and failed, and does not check response.ok, presumably because apiRequest throws on non-OK responses.

symbols.intent: Parse and validate the JSON body of a batch job progress poll into a BatchJobProgressResponse. It guards against malformed or mismatched progress data.
symbols.inputs: response: fetch Response (JSON); expectedJobId: string the poll was made for
symbols.outputs: Promise<BatchJobProgressResponse>, the validated payload returned as-is. Throws Error('Batch progress returned an invalid response') on any violation.
symbols.side_effects: Consumes the response body via response.json().
symbols.invariants: jobId must equal expectedJobId. status must be one of processing, completed or failed. processed, total, success, failed and elapsedMs must be finite, non-negative numbers. failures must be {id, error} entries. currentItem must be a string if present. processed must be <= total. success + failed must be <= processed, and must equal processed once the status is not 'processing'.
symbols.evidence: It is used in pollJobProgress inside useBatchActions. The validation chain is at L175-220.

symbols.intent: Core hook for executing a bulk action. It tracks status (idle, confirming, processing, completed, failed, partial, cancelled), progress, result and error. It calls the batch API, shows toasts, invalidates React Query caches, and exposes confirm, cancel, reset and retryFailed. Progress is either simulated with a timer or polled from a server job.
symbols.inputs: options: { onSuccess, onError, onProgress, simulateProgress=true, pollProgressInterval=1000 }. execute takes a BatchActionConfig { resource, action, ids, data?, messages?, invalidateQueries?, useJobProgress? }.
symbols.outputs: UseBatchActionsReturn: { status, progress, result, error, execute, confirm, cancel, reset, retryFailed, isProcessing, isComplete, pendingConfig }. execute resolves to a BatchResult or rejects with an Error.
symbols.side_effects: Sends HTTP requests via apiRequest (POST, or PUT for update). Starts and stops setInterval timers for simulated progress and for polling. Calls toast. Invalidates queries. Calls the onProgress, onSuccess and onError callbacks.
symbols.invariants: The endpoint is `/api/batch/${resource}/${suffix}` with body {ids, data}. Success is reported only when totalFailed===0. 'partial' means some items succeeded and some failed. 'failed' means every item failed. isComplete is true for completed, partial or failed.
symbols.missing: Several behaviours look incomplete or buggy. (1) The AbortController is created but never passed to apiRequest, so cancel() cannot abort the in-flight request. (2) pollJobProgress only starts a setInterval and returns immediately, so `await pollJobProgress` does not wait for the job. In job mode, toasts, onSuccess and invalidateQueries are never run, and result is not updated with the final job outcome. (3) execute clears pendingConfig on success, so retryFailed (which needs pendingConfig) returns null after a normal run. pendingConfig is only set by confirm(). (4) No unmount cleanup of the intervals. (5) onProgress is called inside a setState updater, which is a side effect. (6) The ETA division can produce Infinity when elapsed is 0. (7) onSuccess is not called in the all-failed case, and onError is not called either.
symbols.evidence: useBatchActions.execute, pollJobProgress, cancel and retryFailed bodies in L222-547. The inventory reports 'stub=empty' with L222-223, but the shown source contains a full implementation, so the inventory range or stub flag looks like an artifact.

.task123-publishing-candidate/external/m.module_purpose: A pure-Python/NumPy emulation layer for CUDA's execution model on the project's 'digital GPU'. It provides Dim3, a per-block shared-memory scratchpad, warp shuffle/reduction helpers, atomics, CUDA-style math and fp16 intrinsics, a per-block CUDARuntime context, and launch_kernel, which loops over the grid and calls a Python kernel function once per block. It is explicitly not a CUDA interpreter. It is the substrate that SM102 kernels, and the CUDAModule wrapper in nvcc.py, are written against.

symbols.evidence: runtime.py L31-54; docstring 'Thread/block/grid dimension triple'

symbols.intent: Store x, y, z, defaulting each to 1.
symbols.invariants: No validation.
symbols.evidence: L35-36. The inventory's long caller list for __init__ appears to be name-collision noise from other classes' constructors.

symbols.evidence: L39-47; used by launch_kernel and CUDAModule.__call__

Model one 32-lane warp holding per-lane float32 values and providing warp-level shuffle and reduction primitives.
symbols.invariants: WARP_SIZE = 32. Its _vals buffer is never used by the shfl or reduce methods, which operate on passed-in arrays.

symbols.intent: Overwrite the first min(len, 32) lane values.
symbols.invariants: Lanes beyond len(values) keep old values.

symbols.inputs: mask: int (ignored), val: 32-element array, offset: int
symbols.outputs: new array of the same shape
symbols.invariants: Assumes len(val) == 32 and 0 <= offset <= 32. Despite the name, it fuses shuffle with add, so it is not a pure CUDA __shfl_down_sync, which only returns the shifted value.

symbols.side_effects: allocates shared memory and a warp
symbols.invariants: _shm is None when shared_n_floats == 0. _atomics is an unused empty dict.

symbols.side_effects: may replace self._shm with a fresh zeroed buffer when absent or too small, discarding old contents
symbols.invariants: Returned buffer has at least n_floats elements, and may be larger. Existing contents are kept if already big enough.
symbols.evidence: L188-191; used by reduction_current_sm102

symbols.intent: Emulate __syncthreads(). It is an intentional no-op because each block runs sequentially and vectorised.
symbols.invariants: Correct only because kernels run one vectorised call per block.
symbols.evidence: L194-196 comment 'no-op: digital GPU runs one thread at a time per block call'. The inventory's 'stub=pass' flag is by design.

symbols.intent: Delegate to WarpState.shfl_down_sync, exposing the warp intrinsic on the runtime context.
symbols.invariants: Inherits the fused shuffle-and-add behaviour and ignored mask.

symbols.intent: Convenience warp-wide sum via WarpState.reduce_sum.
symbols.outputs: array with the sum in lane 0
symbols.evidence: L202-203; used by reduction_redesigned_sm102

symbols.intent: Method wrapper over the module-level atomic_add, so kernels can call rt.atomic_add.
Reciprocal square root, mirroring CUDA's rsqrtf.
symbols.invariants: Not float32 precision, unlike CUDA. x <= 0 gives inf or nan with a NumPy warning.
symbols.evidence: L210-212. No callers are visible here.

symbols.intent: Mirror CUDA's expf, computing the exponential in float32.
Return the larger of two scalars, as CUDA's fmaxf.
symbols.invariants: Python max does not follow NaN semantics.

symbols.intent: Convert an array to float16, mirroring CUDA's fp conversion intrinsics.
Convert an array to float32.

Drive a Python kernel function across a CUDA-style grid. It creates one CUDARuntime per block (z, y, x loop order) and calls kernel_fn(rt, *args). Threads within a block are not iterated: thread_idx is fixed at (0,0,0) because kernels are vectorised across threads.
symbols.inputs: kernel_fn: Callable, grid and block: Dim3/int/tuple, shared_n_floats: int, *args forwarded to the kernel
symbols.side_effects: invokes the kernel, which mutates the output arrays passed in args
symbols.invariants: Blocks run sequentially. Each block gets fresh shared memory. Kernels must be written for the vectorised-thread convention. Kernel return values are ignored.
symbols.evidence: L235-259; the docstring says one Python call per block is exact for SM102 kernels. Callers are CUDAModule.__call__ and the tools/native_simt demos.

open_questions: The module docstring says atomicAdd uses a threading.Lock, but atomic_add does not lock, and _AtomicFloat and CUDARuntime._atomics are unused. Is real multithreaded block execution planned?
WarpState.shfl_down_sync fuses add with shuffle, unlike true CUDA semantics, and ignores the mask. Is this intentional for reduce_sum only?
Many inventory callers (e.g. for __init__, reset, view) look like name-collision artifacts from unrelated classes, so real usage of these is uncertain.

.task123-publishing-candidate/script/dep.module_purpose: Deployment 'executive': a dependency-aware, resource-aware task scheduler for the build and start phases of a Replit VM deployment. It validates a task plan (DAG), adds mandatory build-phase ordering edges, and admits tasks against live CPU, memory and I/O capacity. Each task runs as a detached child process whose descendants are tracked. The executive enforces deadlines and retries, supervises readiness of the application task, and tears down process groups on failure or shutdown signals. It emits a checkpoint JSON on failure. The CLI entrypoint (`main`) wires plans, a per-run state dir, signal binding and an /api/ready probe. A large block comment holds quarantined, malformed duplicate copies of the executor and `main`.

.task123-publishing-candidate/server/lib.module_purpose: Central helper for creating Stripe SDK clients on the server. It resolves environment-appropriate Stripe keys, validates credential shape, lazily constructs and caches a client keyed by the current secret, and optionally routes traffic through an HTTPS proxy. In proxy mode it restricts the destination to api.stripe.com:443 and forces Bearer authorization. It also defines a 503 'not configured' error.

symbols.outputs: string | undefined; the selected secret key, or undefined if none is configured.
symbols.invariants: Selection logic lives in shared/stripeCredentials; this wrapper only supplies env and production flag.
symbols.evidence: L10-12; doc comment 'Resolve the only Stripe key appropriate to this runtime'; calls selectStripeSecretKey(process.env, isProductionEnv()).

symbols.intent: Return the publishable Stripe key for the current runtime, which is safe to expose to the browser.

symbols.invariants: Returns only publishable keys, never secrets (per doc comment).
symbols.evidence: L15-17; doc comment 'Publishable keys are safe to return to the browser'.

symbols.intent: Type guard checking that a value is a plausibly well-formed credential string: non-empty, no leading/trailing whitespace, no CR/LF. It deliberately does not check a key prefix, so proxy-delivered opaque bindings pass.
symbols.invariants: True only for strings with length>0, equal to their trimmed form, and with no newline characters. It validates presence/format, not authenticity.
symbols.evidence: L21-24; comment 'Presence is configuration, not proof of authentication. Proxy-delivered bindings need not expose the provider's key prefix'. Used by lazyStripeClient and createStripeClient.

symbols.invariants: Fixed code and status values; name set to 'StripeUnavailableError'.
symbols.evidence: L26-33; thrown in lazyStripeClient.

symbols.intent: Build a getter that defers Stripe SDK client creation until first use, so importing billing services does not require Stripe configuration. It caches the client and rebuilds it if the secret changes.
symbols.inputs: credential: () => string | undefined (secret supplier); options: Stripe.StripeConfig (default {}).
symbols.outputs: A function () => Stripe that returns the cached or newly created client; throws StripeUnavailableError if the credential is invalid or missing.
symbols.side_effects: Calls credential() on each invocation; creates and caches a Stripe client in closure state.
symbols.invariants: Cache is keyed on the exact secret string; a missing or malformed credential always throws StripeUnavailableError rather than returning a stale client.
symbols.evidence: L36-48; doc comment 'Importing local billing/history services must not require a remote provider'. Inventory shows no callers in this file, presumably used by other modules.

symbols.intent: Create a Stripe SDK client. If HTTPS_PROXY is set, it uses a custom HTTP client that routes via the proxy, allows only api.stripe.com:443 over https, and replaces the Authorization header with a Bearer token so opaque credential bindings are preserved.
symbols.inputs: secret: string; options: Stripe.StripeConfig (default {}). Reads process.env.HTTPS_PROXY.
symbols.outputs: Stripe instance. Throws Error if the credential is invalid; per-request, the proxy transport throws 'Stripe transport destination rejected' for disallowed destinations.
symbols.side_effects: Constructs an HttpsProxyAgent and Node HTTP client when proxying; network requests happen later via the client.
symbols.invariants: The credential is never sent to a host other than api.stripe.com:443 over https in proxy mode. Existing Authorization headers are stripped and replaced. A caller-supplied httpClient in options is overridden in proxy mode (spread order).
symbols.evidence: L50-73; comments 'Never send a credential through a configurable alternate destination' and 'Basic authentication hides opaque bindings from credential substitution. Bearer ...'.

open_questions: The inventory lists no callers for any function, so usage is likely in other modules (this is a '.task123-publishing-candidate' directory); it is unconfirmed whether these exports are wired into the live server.
In proxy mode a caller-supplied options.httpClient is silently overridden; unclear whether that is intended.
The non-proxy path does not restrict destinations, so the destination guard applies only when HTTPS_PROXY is set.

.task123-publishing-candidate/server/ser.module_purpose: Helpers for the backup/restore subsystem to find usable PostgreSQL client binaries (pg_dump, psql) on PATH. They probe each binary's version, ask the target server for its major version, and pick a client at least as new as the server. They also convert a postgres URL into libpq PG* environment variables (so credentials stay off the command line), redact diagnostics, and read the source server version from a dump header. All child processes are bounded by timeout and output size.

symbols.intent: Convert a postgres:// or postgresql:// URL into libpq environment variables (PGHOST, PGPORT, PGUSER, PGDATABASE, optional PGPASSWORD). Whitelisted query parameters are mapped to their PG* variables. Unknown parameters are rejected.
symbols.side_effects: None. Throws on a bad protocol, missing host or database, or an unsupported query parameter.
symbols.invariants: Only whitelisted parameters are accepted. The last repeated query parameter wins and overrides the URL authority/path values. fallback_application_name is used only if PGAPPNAME is unset. IPv6 brackets are stripped from the host. The port defaults to 5432.
symbols.evidence: L35-97; the `supported` map and the comment about URI query override semantics. The password is passed through the environment rather than argv, as used in queryServerMajor.

.task123-publishing-candidate/server/ser.module_purpose: Shared SSRF-safe outbound HTTP fetch utility. It classifies reserved/private IPs, validates that a URL is a public http(s) URL, and fetches text or binary bodies with limits on size, time and redirects. A custom DNS lookup on the http/https Agents rejects private or reserved addresses at connect time, which closes the DNS-rebinding window. The header comment says URL-to-content generation, the URL parser and autopilot link enrichment must use it.

symbols.intent: Decide whether an IP literal (or 'localhost') is private, loopback, link-local, CGNAT, documentation, transition, multicast or otherwise reserved, so it must not be fetched. It fails closed on anything it cannot parse.
symbols.inputs: raw: string. A plain IPv4 or IPv6 address, a bracketed IPv6 address, an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address, or 'localhost'.
symbols.outputs: boolean. True means blocked/reserved. False means a public address.
symbols.side_effects: None. It reads module-level BlockList and regex constants. It recurses once for the dotted ::ffff:a.b.c.d form.
symbols.invariants: Brackets are stripped and the input is lowercased. A condensed-hex ::ffff: form is always blocked. IPv6 is allowed only if it normalizes to a 2xxx: or 3xxx: global-unicast prefix and is not in the reserved IPv6 ranges (2001::/23, 2001:db8::/32, 2002::/16). Unparseable IPv6 is blocked. IPv4 is checked against the reserved BlockList and then PRIVATE_IPV4_RE.
symbols.evidence: safeFetchBuffer.ts L36-63. It is called by safeDnsLookup and assertPublicHttpUrl in the same file. The inventory shows callers=[] only because it counts external callers.

symbols.intent: Replacement for dns.lookup, used as the Agent `lookup` option. It resolves all addresses for a host and refuses the connection if any resolved address is reserved. Checking at connect time defeats DNS rebinding.
symbols.outputs: Via callback. On error it returns an ECONNREFUSED 'SSRF blocked' error, a DNS error, or 'DNS returned no addresses'. On success it returns an array of addresses if options.all is set, otherwise the first address and family.
symbols.side_effects: Performs a DNS lookup. It is a module-private const, not exported.
symbols.invariants: Every resolved address must pass isReservedIp. It rejects if any one of them is reserved, not just the first.
symbols.evidence: L66-95. It is wired into safeHttpAgent and safeHttpsAgent at L97-101.

symbols.intent: Pre-flight validation that a string is a fetchable public http(s) URL. It throws on an invalid URL, a non-http(s) scheme, embedded credentials, localhost/.local/.internal hostnames, or a literal reserved IPv4/IPv6 host.
symbols.outputs: The parsed URL object. It throws Error otherwise ('Invalid URL', 'Only http and https URLs are allowed', 'URLs with embedded credentials are not allowed', 'Blocked host').
symbols.side_effects: None. It does no DNS resolution.
symbols.invariants: This is a literal-host check only. Hostnames that resolve to private IPs are left to the connect-time DNS guard, as the docstring states. Brackets are stripped from IPv6 hosts before checking.
symbols.evidence: L113-142 and the docstring. It is used by safeFetchBuffer and in beforeRedirect. The inventory's callers=[] only reflects the absence of external callers.

symbols.intent: Fetch a public URL and return its body decoded as UTF-8 text, with SSRF, redirect, size and time bounds. It returns non-2xx responses to the caller and throws only on network errors, SSRF blocks or invalid URLs.
symbols.inputs: rawUrl: string. opts: SafeFetchOptions (allowedHost predicate, timeoutMs, maxBytes, headers).
symbols.outputs: Promise<SafeFetchResult> with {url, status, contentType, body: string}.
symbols.invariants: It adds no behavior of its own beyond the UTF-8 decode. All safety comes from safeFetchBuffer.
symbols.evidence: L163-165. The body is a short thin wrapper that delegates to safeFetchBuffer. The inventory's 'stub=empty' is a false positive, because the function really does delegate and decode.

symbols.intent: Core SSRF-safe fetcher. It validates the URL and the optional allowedHost, then does an axios GET with the SSRF-guarded agents, a timeout, a size cap, at most 3 redirects, no proxy, and a browser-like User-Agent. Each redirect hop is re-validated. It returns the raw body as a Buffer.
symbols.inputs: rawUrl: string. opts: SafeFetchOptions. Defaults are timeoutMs 12000 and maxBytes 1,500,000. opts.headers override the default headers.
symbols.outputs: Promise<{url, status, contentType, body: Buffer}>. The URL is the normalized href of the initial request, not the final redirected URL.
symbols.side_effects: Outbound HTTP(S) request. It uses the module-level agents with keepAlive off.
symbols.invariants: validateStatus always returns true, so non-2xx responses do not throw. beforeRedirect rejects credentials, a missing hostname, non-public hosts and hosts not allowed by allowedHost. The connect-time DNS guard is the authoritative check.
symbols.evidence: L171-end. The inventory's 'stub=empty' reflects only the signature lines and is a false positive, since the body is fully implemented. It has no docstring of its own, but the safeFetchText docstring describes both.

open_questions: No callers are visible in the provided context. It is unconfirmed whether the URL-to-content, advanced URL parser and autopilot modules named in the header actually use it, or whether the file under '.task123-publishing-candidate' is a candidate copy that is not yet wired in.

In beforeRedirect, an IPv6 `options.hostname` from follow-redirects may be unbracketed. Building `${proto}//${hostname}` would then throw 'Invalid URL', which fails closed but could wrongly block legitimate IPv6 redirect targets. This was not verified.
The returned `url` is the initial URL, not the final URL after redirects. Callers may expect the final URL.

client/src/hooks/useBatchAction.ts.module_purpose: Client-side React hook layer for running bulk ("batch") operations against `/api/batch/{resource}/{action}`. The core `useBatchAction` hook manages the lifecycle (confirm, execute, progress, result, cancel, reset, retry), shows toasts and invalidates React Query caches. A strict response parser validates the server payload. Five domain wrappers (distribution, social, marketplace, files, analytics) preconfigure resource, action, messages and query keys.

symbols.intent: Read a fetch Response's JSON and validate that it is a well-formed BatchResult consistent with the IDs that were requested, so the UI never trusts a malformed or inconsistent server reply.
symbols.inputs: response: Response (body is JSON); expectedIds: string[] (the IDs sent in the batch request).
symbols.outputs: Promise<BatchResult> with success, failed, totals, and optional downloadUrl, exportId and comparisonData (null or absent values normalised to undefined). Throws Error('Batch operation returned an invalid response') or Error('...results for unexpected items').
symbols.side_effects: Consumes the response body (response.json()). No other effects.
symbols.invariants: Payload must be a non-array object. success must be a string[] and failed an array of {id, error} strings. totalRequested must equal expectedIds.length, totalSucceeded must equal success.length, totalFailed must equal failed.length, and success+failed must cover exactly expectedIds.length items. Every returned ID must be in the requested set. Optional fields must have the right types.
symbols.evidence: Used in useBatchAction.execute (`parseBatchResultResponse(response, ids)`). The inventory's 'stub=None' agrees with the full validating body at L88-151.

symbols.intent: Generic hook that runs a batch action on a list of resource IDs. It exposes status, progress, result and error state plus execute, confirm, cancel, reset and retryFailed. It posts to /api/batch/{resource}/{action}, parses and validates the result, toasts the outcome, and invalidates the listed query keys.
symbols.inputs: options: {onSuccess, onError, onProgress, simulateProgress=true}. execute takes a BatchActionConfig {resource, action, ids, data, successMessage, errorMessage, invalidateQueries}.
symbols.outputs: UseBatchActionReturn: {status, progress, result, error, execute, confirm, cancel, reset, retryFailed, isProcessing, isComplete, pendingConfig}. execute resolves to BatchResult or throws.
symbols.side_effects: Network request via apiRequest (PUT for 'update', POST otherwise). Starts a 200ms setInterval for simulated progress. Fires toasts. Calls queryClient.invalidateQueries. Calls the onSuccess, onError and onProgress callbacks. Updates React state.
symbols.invariants:
Status is completed when totalFailed==0, partial when some succeeded, failed when all failed or on a thrown error. The progress simulation caps at total-1 until the response returns. Progress percentage is derived from current/total.

Known gaps:
- The inventory's 'stub=empty' flag is an artifact; the body is fully implemented.
- AbortController is created but its signal is never passed to apiRequest, so cancel() only changes UI state and does not abort the request. A completing execute can then overwrite the 'cancelled' status.
- execute sets pendingConfig to null on completion, so retryFailed (which requires pendingConfig) will almost always return null after a normal execute.
- When every item fails, onError is not called.
- Query invalidation runs even when everything failed.
- Progress is simulated, not real.
symbols.missing: Pass abortControllerRef.signal to apiRequest and handle abort. Keep the last executed config so retryFailed works. Decide whether onError should fire on total failure. Report real progress if the server supports it.
symbols.evidence: execute: `setPendingConfig(null)` before return. retryFailed: `if (!pendingConfig || !result || ...) return null`. abortControllerRef created in execute but `apiRequest(method, url, body)` has no signal. cancel() calls abort() on that ref.

symbols.intent: Wrapper around useBatchAction offering release-specific batch operations for the music distribution feature: submit, takedown, update and delete releases.
symbols.inputs: options: UseBatchActionOptions. Returned functions take ids: string[], plus data for submit and update.
symbols.outputs: The full useBatchAction return value plus submitReleases, takedownReleases, updateReleases and deleteReleases, each returning Promise<BatchResult>.
symbols.side_effects: Calls batchAction.execute on resource 'releases' (network, toasts), then invalidates '/api/distribution/releases'.
symbols.invariants: Resource is always 'releases'. Messages and invalidation keys are fixed. The useCallbacks depend on the whole batchAction object, which is a new object every render, so the memoization is ineffective.
symbols.evidence: L390-L460 bodies define the four callbacks; the inventory 'stub=empty' is a parse artifact. No callers are visible in this file.

symbols.inputs: options; ids, plus scheduledTime for schedulePosts and data for updatePosts.
symbols.outputs: The useBatchAction return plus schedulePosts, deletePosts and updatePosts.
symbols.side_effects: Executes batch calls on resource 'posts'. Invalidates '/api/social/posts' and, for schedule and delete, '/api/social/calendar'.
symbols.invariants: scheduledTime is passed through as data.scheduledTime without validation.

symbols.outputs: The useBatchAction return plus updateListings, deleteListings, updatePrices and updateLicenses.
symbols.side_effects: Batch calls on resource 'marketplace' with action 'update' or 'delete'. Invalidates '/api/marketplace/beats' and '/api/marketplace/my-beats'.
symbols.invariants: updatePrices and updateLicenses are just 'update' with a single-field data payload. Price is not validated client-side.
symbols.evidence: The body defines the four callbacks; the inventory 'stub=empty' is an artifact.

symbols.intent: Wrapper around useBatchAction for bulk file management: delete, move to a folder, prepare a download and update metadata.
symbols.inputs: options; ids, plus folder for moveFiles and data for updateFiles.
symbols.outputs: The useBatchAction return plus deleteFiles, moveFiles, downloadFiles and updateFiles.
symbols.side_effects: Batch calls on resource 'files'. Delete and move invalidate '/api/files/list', '/api/files/storage-usage' and '/api/storage/quota'. update invalidates '/api/files/list'. download invalidates nothing.
symbols.invariants: downloadFiles only prepares a download. The caller must read result.downloadUrl itself; the hook does not trigger the download.

symbols.intent: Wrapper around useBatchAction for batch analytics operations: exporting data and generating comparisons across items.
symbols.inputs: options; ids, plus format (default 'csv') and optional dateRange for export.
symbols.outputs: The useBatchAction return plus exportAnalytics and compareAnalytics. Results may carry downloadUrl, exportId or comparisonData.
symbols.side_effects: Batch calls on resource 'analytics' with actions 'export' and 'compare'. No query invalidation.
symbols.invariants: Both actions are read-only, so no cache invalidation is needed.
symbols.evidence: The body defines both callbacks; the BatchResult type includes exportId and comparisonData, which fit these actions. The inventory 'stub=empty' is an artifact.

open_questions: The inventory shows no callers for any exported hook. Are they used by pages or components outside this module's analysis, or are they dead?
Does the server's /api/batch/* API actually return the strict shape parseBatchResultResponse requires? Duplicate IDs in a request would fail validation.
Does apiRequest throw on non-2xx responses? The parser does not check response.ok.
Are the 'process' action and the other unused BatchActionType values (e.g. 'withdraw') used anywhere?
Should retryFailed work after execute? As written, pendingConfig is cleared on completion, which looks like a bug.

client/src/hooks/useBatchActions.ts.module_purpose: React hook library for bulk operations on resources (releases, tracks, posts, beats, analytics). A generic `useBatchActions` hook drives a state machine (idle/confirming/processing/completed/partial/failed/cancelled). It POSTs or PUTs `{ids, data}` to `/api/batch/{resource}/{action}`, strictly validates the response, tracks real or simulated progress, shows toasts and invalidates React Query caches. Domain wrappers bind it to specific resources. The file also re-exports legacy hooks from `./useBatchAction`.

symbols.intent: Parse and strictly validate the JSON body of a batch endpoint response into a `BatchResult`. It checks shape, that counts are consistent with the requested ids, and that every returned id was actually requested. It guards the UI against malformed or mismatched server responses.
symbols.inputs: response: fetch Response; expectedIds: string[] (the ids sent in the request).
symbols.outputs: Promise<BatchResult> with success, failed, totals and optional downloadUrl, exportId, comparisonData and jobId. Throws Error('Batch operation returned an invalid response') or '...unexpected items' otherwise.
symbols.side_effects: Consumes the response body via response.json().
symbols.invariants: success and failed are disjoint-by-count and sum to expectedIds.length. The totals fields equal the array lengths. All ids are in the requested set. Optional string fields are string, null or undefined. comparisonData is an array if present. Duplicate ids are not checked.
symbols.evidence: Used in useBatchActions.execute (`parseBatchActionsResponse(response, ids)`); validation logic L110-173.

symbols.intent: Validate the JSON body of a batch job progress poll (`/api/batch/progress/{jobId}`) and return it typed as `BatchJobProgressResponse`. It enforces numeric sanity and internal consistency (processed <= total, success+failed <= processed, equal when not processing).
symbols.outputs: Promise<BatchJobProgressResponse>. Throws Error('Batch progress returned an invalid response') on any violation, including a jobId mismatch.
symbols.invariants: status is one of processing, completed or failed. Numeric fields are finite and >= 0. failures entries have string id and error. Once the job is no longer processing, success+failed == processed.
symbols.evidence: Called in pollJobProgress inside useBatchActions; L175-220.

symbols.intent: Core hook for running confirmable bulk actions against `/api/batch/:resource/:action`. It exposes status, progress, result and error. `execute` runs the action. `confirm` stages a config for a confirmation step. `cancel`, `reset` and `retryFailed` manage the lifecycle. It simulates progress by default or polls a server job when `useJobProgress` is set. It toasts, invalidates queries and calls the onSuccess/onError callbacks.
symbols.inputs: options: onSuccess, onError, onProgress, simulateProgress (default true), pollProgressInterval (default 1000ms).
symbols.outputs: UseBatchActionsReturn: status, progress, result, error, execute, confirm, cancel, reset, retryFailed, isProcessing, isComplete, pendingConfig.
symbols.side_effects: Network requests via apiRequest. setInterval timers for simulation and polling. Toasts. queryClient.invalidateQueries. Many state updates.
symbols.invariants: HTTP method and URL come from a per-action map (only `update` uses PUT) and fall back to POST with the action name as suffix. `execute` rethrows errors after setting failed state. Progress percentage and ETA are recomputed on every update.
symbols.missing: Several defects. (1) The job-progress branch returns from `execute` before polling finishes. It never fires toast, onSuccess or invalidateQueries on completion, and the polling interval is never cleared on unmount. (2) The AbortController is created but its signal is never passed to apiRequest, so `cancel` does not abort the request. (3) `execute` clears pendingConfig on success, so `retryFailed` (which requires pendingConfig) effectively returns null unless confirm is called again. (4) The parser requires success+failed to equal the requested count, which seems incompatible with an asynchronous job response that is still in progress. (5) The async setInterval callback can overlap requests. (6) Simulated progress is cosmetic.
symbols.evidence: L222-547 `execute`, `cancel`, `retryFailed`, `pollJobProgress`. The inventory's 'stub=empty' reflects only the L222-223 signature range; the body is a full implementation.

symbols.intent: Convenience wrapper over useBatchActions for distribution releases. It offers submitReleases, deleteReleases and updateReleases, each with preset messages and invalidation of `/api/distribution/releases`.
symbols.inputs: options: UseBatchActionsOptions; the returned callbacks take ids and, for submit and update, data.

symbols.side_effects: Triggers batch network calls and query invalidation through execute.
symbols.invariants: resource is always 'releases'.

client/src/hooks/useBulkAction.ts.module_purpose: React hooks for running bulk operations (delete, update, export, status change, submit, withdraw, schedule, process) against /api/batch/:resource/* endpoints. They manage a confirm/process/result state machine, progress, toasts, and React Query invalidation. The module also validates the server's bulk-result response.

symbols.intent: Parse and strictly validate a bulk-operation HTTP response, ensuring the payload is consistent with the requested IDs, and return a typed BulkActionResult.

symbols.side_effects: Consumes the response body via response.json(). No other side effects.
symbols.invariants: Payload is a non-array object. success is a string[]. failed is an array of {id: string, error: string}. totalRequested equals expectedIds.length. totalSucceeded and totalFailed equal the array lengths. success plus failed counts equal the requested count. Every returned ID is in expectedIds. Duplicates are not checked.
symbols.evidence: Called inside useBulkAction.execute (L~200) as parseBulkActionResponse(response, ids). The inventory shows callers=[] only because the call is intra-file. Validation logic L76-121.

symbols.intent: Core hook that exposes a bulk-action state machine (idle/confirming/processing/completed/partial/failed). It maps an action type to an API endpoint and method, runs the request, validates the result, updates progress, shows toasts, invalidates queries, and fires callbacks.
symbols.inputs: options: {onSuccess, onError, onProgress}. execute takes a BulkActionConfig {resource, action, ids, data, successMessage, errorMessage, invalidateQueries}.
symbols.outputs: {status, progress, result, error, execute, confirm, cancel, reset, isProcessing, pendingConfig}. execute resolves to a BulkActionResult and rejects on error.
symbols.side_effects: Issues a network request via apiRequest. Sets React state. Shows toasts. Calls queryClient.invalidateQueries for each key. Creates and clears an AbortController. Clears pendingConfig in finally.
symbols.invariants: update and status_change share the PUT /update endpoint. All other actions use POST. An unknown action throws. Progress is only set to 0 and then to total, with no intermediate steps. Invalidation is skipped when the request throws. When every item fails, onSuccess is not called and execute still resolves. For partial results, onSuccess is called. The AbortController signal is never passed to apiRequest, so cancel() cannot actually abort the request. The file has // @ts-nocheck.
symbols.missing: The abort signal is not wired into apiRequest, so cancel during processing only resets UI state. Progress is not granular. confirmMessage is carried in the config but never used by the hook. Invalidation does not run on thrown errors.
symbols.evidence: abortControllerRef is created in execute but never passed to apiRequest. updateProgress is called only at start and end. confirm() sets pendingConfig/status. The switch in execute L~160-205.

symbols.side_effects: Triggers a PUT /api/batch/{resource}/update call, toasts, and query invalidation.

It also defines default shortcut tables with no-op handlers and thin per-module wrapper hooks that let callers override handlers by shortcut id.

symbols.outputs: {shortcuts: ShortcutDefinition[]} from getShortcutsByContext(module), memoized on module and getShortcutsByContext.
symbols.side_effects: Calls useShortcutContext(module). In an effect it calls registerShortcut for each non-disabled shortcut with id `${module}.${id}`, and unregisters them all on cleanup or dependency change.

client/src/lib/a11y/focus.ts.module_purpose: Accessibility focus-management helpers for the React client. It covers saving and restoring focus and scroll position (including a stack-based singleton `focusManager`), moving focus within a container, computing next and previous focusable elements with wrap-around, applying custom focus-ring styles, editing tabindex, checking whether an element is focusable, and a focus scope that blocks tab access to elements outside a container (modal-style focus trap). It depends on `getFocusableElements` from `@/lib/accessibility`, which was not available for review. The inventory shows no callers for any symbol, but this is a library module and exports may be consumed elsewhere.

symbols.intent: Snapshot the currently focused element and window scroll position so they can be restored later, for example when a modal or dialog closes.
symbols.outputs: FocusRestoreState {element: document.activeElement or null, scrollPosition {x, y}}
symbols.side_effects: None. It reads document and window.
symbols.invariants: The element is whatever was active at call time, possibly body.
symbols.evidence: focus.ts L8-16; used by FocusManager.push; the FocusRestoreState interface.

symbols.intent: Return focus to a previously saved element if it is still in the DOM, then restore the saved scroll position.
symbols.side_effects: Calls element.focus() and window.scrollTo(). Scrolling happens even when the element is gone.
symbols.invariants: Focus is only restored if document.body still contains the element. The excessive optional chaining on `state?.` means a null state would still throw at `state?.scrollPosition.x`.
symbols.evidence: focus.ts L18-23; called by FocusManager.pop.

symbols.intent: Singleton that keeps a stack of saved focus states, supporting nested overlays that each restore focus on close.
symbols.inputs: none (the constructor is implicitly public, but getInstance is the intended access path)
symbols.side_effects: Holds module-level state. push reads the DOM. pop schedules restoration via requestAnimationFrame.
symbols.invariants: The stack is LIFO. Restoration is deferred one animation frame. `depth` reports the stack size.
symbols.evidence: focus.ts L25-58. Methods are push, pop, clear, depth and getInstance. The constructor is not private, so the singleton is not strictly enforced.

symbols.intent: Focus the first focusable descendant of a container. If there is none, make the container itself programmatically focusable and focus it.
symbols.outputs: true if a focusable child was focused, false if it fell back to the container
symbols.side_effects: Calls .focus(). In the fallback it sets tabindex=-1 on the container.
symbols.invariants: Relies on getFocusableElements returning an array-like of elements in order. Returns false even though the container fallback received focus.

symbols.invariants: Valid range is 0 <= index < count.
symbols.evidence: focus.ts L80-87.

symbols.outputs: The next element, the first element if current is last or not found, or null if there are none
symbols.invariants: Wraps circularly. A current element not in the list yields the first element.

symbols.intent: Return the previous focusable element before the current one in the container, wrapping around to the last.

symbols.evidence: focus.ts L218-235.

symbols.invariants: Previous tabindex values are saved and restored, and the attribute is removed if there was none.

symbols.side_effects: Queries the document and mutates attributes on external elements.

The selector matches a[href], button, input, textarea and select regardless of tabindex, so a second lock() would record '-1' as the original and unlock would then restore -1. It also misses elements added after locking and does not set inert or aria-hidden.

symbols.intent: Restore the original tabindex of every element that lock() disabled and clear the marker attribute.

symbols.evidence: focus.ts L261-271.

open_questions: No callers appear in the inventory. It is unknown whether these exports are used elsewhere, such as in dialogs or components, or whether the module is dead code that duplicates helpers in @/lib/accessibility.
The behavior of getFocusableElements in @/lib/accessibility (return type, ordering, filtering) was not available. The array methods used here assume it returns a real Array.

client/src/lib/a11y/keyboard.ts.module_purpose: Keyboard-accessibility helpers for the client: a modal focus trap, a roving-tabindex controller for composite widgets (lists, toolbars, grids), a document-level Escape handler, simple arrow-key navigation within a container, and a typeahead matcher. Each setup function returns either a controller object or a cleanup function that removes its listeners.

symbols.intent: Build a focus trap for a container (modal or dialog). While active, Tab and Shift+Tab wrap between the first and last focusable elements, outside clicks are blocked unless allowed, Escape calls a callback, and focus returns to the previously focused element on deactivate.
symbols.inputs: container: HTMLElement; options: FocusTrapOptions (initialFocus element or selector, returnFocusOnDeactivate=true, escapeDeactivates=true, onEscape, allowOutsideClick=false)
symbols.side_effects: None at creation. The returned methods register or remove document listeners and move focus.
symbols.invariants: Listeners exist only between activate and deactivate. activate and deactivate are idempotent. Closure state (active, paused, previouslyFocused) is per instance.
symbols.evidence: L18-129. The inventory flags this as an empty stub, but the body is fully implemented. No callers appear in this file.

symbols.intent: Document keydown listener that routes Tab to the wrap logic and Escape to the onEscape callback while the trap is active and not paused.
symbols.invariants: Does nothing when inactive or paused. On Escape it calls onEscape but does not call deactivate itself, even though the option is named escapeDeactivates. The caller is presumably expected to deactivate.
symbols.missing: Escape does not deactivate the trap. The option name implies it should, unless the caller does so inside onEscape.

symbols.intent: Wrap focus from the last element to the first on Tab, and from the first to the last on Shift+Tab.
symbols.invariants: Returns early when the container has no focusable elements. It only intervenes when focus is exactly on the first or last element, so focus that is already outside the container is not pulled back.

symbols.side_effects: preventDefault, stopPropagation, focuses the first element
symbols.invariants: Skipped when inactive, paused, or allowOutsideClick is true.

symbols.side_effects: Focuses an element and may set tabindex=-1 on the container.
symbols.invariants: If initialFocus is a selector that does not match, nothing is focused and there is no fallback.

symbols.intent: Turn the trap on: remember the currently focused element, attach listeners, and focus into the container on the next animation frame.
symbols.side_effects: Adds document keydown and capture click listeners, calls requestAnimationFrame, and changes focus.
symbols.invariants: No-op if already active.

symbols.intent: Turn the trap off, remove listeners, and optionally restore focus to the previously focused element.
symbols.invariants: No-op if inactive.

symbols.intent: Temporarily suspend the trap's handlers without removing them.
symbols.invariants: None.

symbols.intent: Resume a paused trap.

script/deployment/executive.mjs.module_purpose: Deployment 'executive': a dependency-aware, resource-admitting task scheduler for the build and start phases of the Max Booster deployment. It validates a task plan, adds build-phase ordering edges, spawns each task as a detached process group, and admits tasks against live CPU, memory and I/O capacity. It enforces per-task and overall deadlines, retries on selected signals with backoff, probes application readiness, and tears down process trees on exit. The CLI entrypoint `main('build'|'start')` wires up the plan, signal binding, a temp state dir, and failure checkpoint reporting. A large block comment in the middle holds quarantined, malformed duplicate copies of the scheduler tail and of `main`; the live code is the part above the comment plus the final `main` below it.

symbols.intent: Monotonic millisecond clock (performance.now) used for all scheduler timing, so deadlines are unaffected by wall-clock changes.
symbols.invariants: monotonic
symbols.evidence: L15; used throughout runExecutive/stopJob. The listed callers are unrelated Python files with a name collision.

symbols.intent: Send a signal to an entire process group (negative pid), ignoring groups that are already gone.
symbols.side_effects: process.kill(-pid, signal); swallows ESRCH, rethrows other errors
symbols.invariants: No-op for non-integer pids or pid < 2, so it never signals init or the caller's own group
symbols.evidence: L17-24; used by stopJob with detached:true spawns, which make the child a group leader

symbols.intent: List live (non-zombie, non-dead) processes whose process-group id equals the given pid, by scanning /proc.
symbols.side_effects: Reads /proc/*/stat; tolerates ENOENT/ESRCH/EACCES races, rethrows other errors
symbols.invariants: Excludes states Z and X; the regex handles a comm field containing parentheses; fields[2] is pgrp (the third field after the comm)
symbols.evidence: L26-50; used in stopJob to poll for group exit. Linux-only (/proc).

symbols.inputs: operation function (sync or async), ms, label for the error message
symbols.outputs: Promise resolving to the operation's result
symbols.side_effects: Sets and clears a timer. The operation itself is not cancelled on timeout.
symbols.invariants: Timer is always cleared in finally
symbols.evidence: L52-67; used for owned.stop cleanup and the readiness probe, where the code checks error.code === 'DEPLOY_OPERATION_TIMEOUT'

symbols.intent: Reliably stop a task job: first the owned-process tracker (which also covers descendants in other sessions), then the whole process group with SIGTERM then SIGKILL. Throws if members are still alive afterwards.
symbols.outputs: Promise<void>; rejects on leftover processes or a deferred tracker error
symbols.side_effects: Signals processes and sleeps while polling. The application task gets a 26s grace period, others 5s; there is a 250ms group deadline when a tracker exists.
symbols.invariants: The tracker error is thrown only after group cleanup has been attempted; the SIGKILL window is 1.5s
symbols.evidence: L69-113; called from the main loop on failed jobs and in the finally drain. The comment in the quarantined text says a group-only kill misses sidecars that create their own sessions.

symbols.intent: Core scheduler. It runs a validated plan of tasks as detached child processes, respecting dependencies and live capacity (CPU slots, memory reservation, I/O slots). It supports elastic CPU sharing, retries with exponential backoff on selected signals, a global budget and per-task deadlines, readiness polling for the application task, abort-signal handling, admission timeout, and guaranteed cleanup of children. On failure it attaches checkpoint metadata to the error.
symbols.inputs: tasks, options {cwd, env, capacity, budgetMs, pollMs, admissionTimeoutMs, log, signal, readiness}
symbols.side_effects: Spawns processes, logs progress every 15s, creates owned-process trackers, drains and kills children in finally, and may throw a cleanup error if there was no primary error
symbols.invariants: Admits at least one task regardless of the soft 80% memory/I/O limits when nothing is active; never exceeds floor(cpus) CPU; once ready, the global budget and application task timeouts stop applying; the primary error takes precedence, with cleanup errors attached as cleanupError

symbols.intent: Live CLI entrypoint. For mode 'build' or 'start' it builds and validates the plan and creates a temp state dir. It binds shutdown signals and computes the budget (minus bootstrap elapsed time for build). It logs detected resources, runs runExecutive (with an /api/ready readiness probe in start mode), and on failure prints a JSON task checkpoint to stderr and rethrows. Finally it unbinds signals, removes the state dir and bootstrap dir, and terminates the boot stub pid.

symbols.outputs: Promise<void>; the invoker sets process.exitCode=1 on failure
symbols.side_effects: Creates and removes a temp dir; registers signal handlers; spawns tasks; fetches localhost /api/ready; removes /tmp/deployment-tools.* bootstrap dirs (regex-guarded); SIGTERMs the boot stub pid
symbols.invariants: Cleanup always runs in finally; the bootstrap rm is restricted to a matching /tmp path; readiness requires HTTP 200, status 'ok', and unifiedAwareness.ready === true

script/lib/provisionPortablePython.mjs.module_purpose: Provisions an isolated, pinned portable CPython (python-build-standalone 3.12.13, x86_64 linux gnu) into <root>/python_runtime. It reuses an existing runtime if it passes verification. Otherwise it downloads and validates the archive, extracts it into a staging dir, installs and verifies locked dependencies, and swaps the staged runtime in with backup/rollback. It can be run as a CLI script or imported.

symbols.intent: Thin synchronous wrapper around spawnSync that runs an external command, throws on spawn error or non-zero exit (including the last 2000 chars of stderr), and returns stdout as a string.
symbols.inputs: commandName string, args array, options {cwd, env, timeout (default 30 min), stdio (default 'pipe')}
symbols.outputs: stdout string (empty if stdio is inherited)
symbols.side_effects: Spawns a child process; with stdio 'inherit' output goes to the parent's console.
symbols.invariants: Non-zero exit or spawn error always throws. 64MB maxBuffer. Default timeout is 30 minutes.
symbols.evidence: L13-28. The inventory's 'stub=empty' flag and its callers (Python files such as team.py and remediation.py) are false positives from name matching on a generic name; the body is fully implemented and used as the default `run` at L97.

symbols.intent: Downloads the release tarball with curl, with HTTPS-only enforcement, TLS 1.2 minimum, retries, and connect and total timeouts.
symbols.outputs: none (the archive is written to destination)
symbols.side_effects: Network request; writes the file at destination.
symbols.invariants: Only HTTPS, including after redirects. Fails on HTTP errors (--fail). Max 180s per curl call, with a 210s process timeout.
symbols.evidence: L30-37. It is the default `download` in provisionPortablePython (L98). There is no integrity or checksum verification of the download.

symbols.intent: Safety-checks the tarball listing before extraction. It requires python/bin/python3 and rejects any member that is absolute, uses '..' traversal, or lies outside the 'python/' root.
symbols.outputs: none; throws Error on invalid archive
symbols.invariants: Every member is 'python' or under 'python/'. No absolute paths or parent traversal. Does not inspect symlink or hardlink targets.
symbols.evidence: L39-57, called at L121.

symbols.intent: Verifies a runtime directory. It checks that bin/python3 is an executable regular file, that its version matches the expected one, and that the dependency installer script passes in --verify-only mode.
symbols.inputs: runtime dir, expectedVersion, repo root, optional run function (injectable for tests)
symbols.side_effects: Executes the runtime's python (version check, then verify-only dependency script, 120s timeout) with cwd=root.
symbols.invariants: Version output must equal exactly 'Python <expectedVersion>'. Python runs isolated (-I -B).
symbols.evidence: L59-72, used at L108 for the existing runtime and L134 for the staged runtime.

symbols.intent: Swaps the staged runtime into place with rollback. The existing runtime directory is renamed to a UUID-named backup, the staged one is renamed into place, and the backup is deleted on success. On failure the backup is restored.
symbols.side_effects: Filesystem renames and a recursive delete of the backup.
symbols.invariants: An existing runtime must be a real directory, not a symlink. If the swap fails and the runtime path is missing, the backup is restored. Rename atomicity requires staged and target to be on the same filesystem; the stage dir is created under root, so this normally holds.
symbols.evidence: L74-92, called at L136. The lstat and existsSync check at L78 is somewhat redundant but harmless.

symbols.intent: Main entry point. It ensures <root>/python_runtime holds a verified portable Python at the pinned version. It reuses the existing runtime if it passes full verification. Otherwise it stages a fresh download, validates it, extracts it, installs and verifies dependencies, and atomically replaces the runtime. The staging dir is always cleaned up.
symbols.inputs: root path, options {version, url, run, download}; the run and download overrides allow test injection
symbols.side_effects: Creates and removes a temp staging directory under root. Downloads from the network. Installs dependencies. Replaces python_runtime. Logs to the console.
symbols.invariants: python_runtime must not be a symlink or a non-directory. A failed existing runtime is kept until the replacement passes. Staging is removed in `finally`. The inventory 'stub=empty' flag is a false positive from line-based detection (L94 is only the signature line).
symbols.evidence: L94-142. The CLI guard at L144-152 sets exitCode=1 on failure and prints that the existing runtime was not replaced.

The release URL is hard-coded to x86_64 linux gnu. Behavior on other platforms is unhandled.

scripts/database-recovery-drill.mjs.module_purpose: Top-level executable script that runs a live database recovery drill. It takes a read-only, repeatable-read snapshot of the Neon primary database, dumps it with pg_dump at that exported snapshot, and optionally retains the dump in private managed storage. It then restores the dump into a disposable loopback-only local PostgreSQL cluster and compares schema fingerprints, per-table row counts and content hashes. Finally it writes sanitized Markdown and JSON reports and sets the process exit code on failure.

symbols.invariants: Only values of length >= 3 are kept, so very short values are not used as redaction patterns.

scripts/readiness-assembled-acceptance.m.module_purpose: Sealed, self-contained 'assembled acceptance' drill for the Max Booster readiness work. Run via `env -i ... node scripts/readiness-assembled-acceptance.mjs [--http-load]`, it refuses to start if sensitive env vars are inherited. scripts/test-data-runtime.mjs.module_purpose: Standalone boundary/integration test script for the data-runtime layer. Run with a clean environment (`env -i PATH=... node scripts/test-data-runtime.mjs`), it uses esbuild to bundle real server modules with external I/O replaced by in-memory mocks. It covers four areas: authoritative session store and revocation (D6), BullMQ retention-worker quarantine (D7), PDIM RedisStore snapshot/AOF recovery and legacy conversion (D4), and database backup/restore plus scheduler shutdown semantics (D1-D3). Failures surface as assert exceptions; success prints PASS lines. Several 'symbols' in the inventory are not real module functions. They are fragments of JavaScript source held in template-literal mocks, or small local helpers.

server/services/backup/postgresTools.ts.module_purpose: Helpers for the backup/restore system that safely locate and choose compatible PostgreSQL client binaries (pg_dump, psql). They convert a DB URL into libpq environment variables so credentials stay off the command line, discover candidate binaries on PATH, and probe their versions. They ask the server for its major version via `SHOW server_version_num`, pick a client whose major is at least the server's, and read the source version from a dump header to guard against restoring into an older server.

server/services/safeUrlFetch.ts.module_purpose: Shared SSRF-safe outbound HTTP(S) fetch utility. It validates URLs, blocks private/reserved IPs (including at connect time through a custom DNS lookup on http/https Agents, which closes DNS-rebinding gaps), re-validates redirect hops, and bounds time, size and redirects. Exposes text and buffer fetchers for any code fetching attacker-influenced URLs.

symbols.intent: Decide whether an IP literal (or 'localhost') is private, loopback, link-local, CGNAT, reserved, documentation or transition-range, and so unsafe to fetch. Fails closed on unparseable or non-global-unicast IPv6.
symbols.inputs: raw: string, an IPv4/IPv6 literal, possibly bracketed or IPv4-mapped IPv6, any case.
symbols.outputs: boolean: true if blocked/reserved, false if public.
symbols.side_effects: None. Reads module-level regexes and the BlockList.
symbols.invariants: Conservative. Condensed hex IPv4-mapped (::ffff:xxxx) is always blocked. IPv6 outside 2000::/3 is blocked. Unparseable IPv6 is blocked. Recurses once for dotted IPv4-mapped addresses.
symbols.evidence: Doc comment L33-35; used by safeDnsLookup and assertPublicHttpUrl in the same file. The inventory lists callers=[] but internal callers exist.

symbols.intent: Pre-flight validation that a string is a well-formed public http(s) URL without credentials and with a non-local, non-reserved literal host. Returns the parsed URL.
symbols.outputs: URL object. Throws Error('Invalid URL'), 'Only http and https URLs are allowed', 'URLs with embedded credentials are not allowed', or 'Blocked host'.
symbols.invariants: Rejects localhost and the .localhost/.local/.internal suffixes. Rejects literal reserved IPv4/IPv6 hosts. Hostnames that resolve to private IPs are not caught here; the connect-time DNS guard handles those.
symbols.evidence: Doc comment L106-112; called by safeFetchBuffer and in beforeRedirect.

symbols.intent: Fetch a public URL and return its body decoded as UTF-8 text, with SSRF, redirect, size and time bounds. Non-2xx responses are returned rather than thrown.
symbols.inputs: rawUrl: string; opts: SafeFetchOptions (allowedHost, timeoutMs, maxBytes, headers).
symbols.outputs: Promise<SafeFetchResult> with url, status, contentType, body string. Rejects on network error, SSRF block, invalid URL or disallowed host.
symbols.invariants: Defaults inherited from safeFetchBuffer. Body is always decoded as utf8 regardless of charset.
symbols.evidence: Body is a thin wrapper that calls safeFetchBuffer and converts the buffer (L163-165). The inventory's 'stub=empty' flag is wrong, since the body is not empty.

symbols.intent: Core SSRF-hardened GET returning raw bytes. Validates the URL, applies an optional host allowlist, and uses guarded agents with no proxy, a timeout, a size cap, at most 3 redirects, and per-redirect re-validation.
symbols.inputs: rawUrl: string; opts: SafeFetchOptions. Defaults are timeoutMs=12000 and maxBytes=1.5MB. Custom headers override the defaults.
symbols.outputs: Promise of {url, status, contentType, body: Buffer}. Throws on invalid or blocked URLs, disallowed destinations, network errors, timeouts or oversize responses.
symbols.side_effects: Outbound HTTP GET using safeHttpAgent/safeHttpsAgent. Uses AbortSignal.timeout.
symbols.invariants: validateStatus accepts all statuses. proxy:false prevents proxy bypass of the DNS guard. beforeRedirect rejects credentials, a missing host and non-public or disallowed hosts. keepAlive is off.
symbols.evidence: L171-173 and the following body; doc comment on safeFetchText describes the behavior. The inventory's 'stub=empty' flag is wrong.

open_questions: The inventory shows no external callers; the header names URL→content generation, the advanced URL parser and autopilot enrichment, but this cannot be verified from this file.
In beforeRedirect only protocol and hostname are re-checked, not the port, and a redirect hop to a hostname relies on the DNS guard.
The safeDnsLookup callback with all:true is cast; compatibility across Node versions was not verified.

project.architecture: Max Booster is a TypeScript monorepo (Express API server, React/Vite client, shared schema) deployed on Replit with Neon Postgres. A Redis-compatible layer (PDIM) provides cache/state. Python-based MaxCore AI services sit beside it, including a software 'digital GPU' that emulates CUDA in NumPy behind an abstract Backend interface. Node .mjs scripts handle deployment scheduling, portable Python provisioning, DB recovery drills and sealed acceptance harnesses. The client holds batch/bulk-action hooks, shortcut hooks, a11y helpers and a video template compiler. The server holds Stripe, SSRF-safe fetch and Postgres-tool helpers. This synthesis comes from module summaries only; I did not inspect function bodies, so the statuses below reflect those summaries.

features.name: CUDA emulation runtime (digital GPU)
features.description: NumPy emulation of CUDA execution: dim3, per-block shared memory, warp shuffle/reduce, atomics, math and fp16 intrinsics, and a per-block CUDARuntime context for SM102 kernels. It appears in several duplicated copies of the repo tree.

features.name: Abstract compute Backend interface
features.description: ABC defining primitive kernels (create_tensor, gemm, add, relu, softmax, attention, conv2d, mlp, reduce) plus defaults, which every DigitalGPU backend must implement.

features.name: Future backends (cluster/ASIC) plug-points
features.description: Deliberately non-functional backends that report is_available()=False and raise NotImplementedError with a documented contract. This is an intentional stub, not a defect.

features.name: AI director analytics feedback loop
features.description: PerformanceRecord dataclass, a pluggable AnalyticsSource protocol with JSONL file and PDIM-backed implementations, feeding observed engagement back to the director.

features.name: Advanced video renderer orchestration
features.description: Generates hook/body/CTA copy and sentiment, submits sync or async video jobs to the MaxCore AI server and polls for results.

features.name: Batch/bulk action client hooks
features.description: Three overlapping React hook libraries (useBatchAction, useBatchActions, useBulkAction) that run bulk operations against /api/batch/{resource}/{action} with confirm/execute/progress/result state machines. The overlap suggests duplication.

features.name: Module keyboard shortcuts
features.description: Hook that registers per-module shortcut tables (studio, analytics, social, distribution, marketplace) with ShortcutContext.

features.name: Accessibility focus and keyboard utilities
features.description: Focus save/restore with a stack manager, focus movement, a modal focus trap, roving tabindex, Escape handler and arrow-key navigation.

features.name: Promo video template compiler
features.description: Compiles promo template options (release, tour, bts, quote, countdown, split, teaser) into a renderer-ready VideoProject.

features.name: Deployment executive scheduler
features.description: Dependency-aware, resource-admitting DAG scheduler for the build and start phases, including plan validation and build-phase ordering edges.

features.name: Portable Python provisioning
features.description: Provisions a pinned python-build-standalone CPython into python_runtime, reusing a verified existing runtime or downloading a new one.

features.name: Database recovery drill
features.description: Takes a repeatable-read snapshot of the Neon primary, runs pg_dump at the exported snapshot, optionally retains the dump, and verifies recovery.

features.name: Sealed acceptance and runtime test harnesses
features.description: Env-scrubbed acceptance drills (readiness, page80) and a mocked data-runtime boundary test, all built with esbuild bundling.

features.name: Stripe client helper
features.description: Resolves environment-appropriate Stripe keys, validates credential shape, and lazily builds and caches a client.

features.name: Postgres client tool selection
features.description: Locates pg_dump and psql on PATH, probes their versions against the server major version, and picks compatible binaries, passing credentials via libpq env vars.

features.name: SSRF-safe URL fetch
features.description: Validates public http(s) URLs, blocks private/reserved IPs including at connect time via a custom DNS lookup (closing DNS rebinding), with size, time and redirect limits.

features.name: Bundled cluster fixture
features.description: esbuild-bundled test fixture inlining server code (log sanitization, PDIM/Redis-compatible client) in a temp cluster-test directory. It is a generated artifact, not source.

Several defects. (1) The job-progress branch returns from `execute` before polling finishes. It never fires toast, onSuccess or invalidateQueries on completion, and the polling interval is never cleared on unmount. (2) The AbortController is created but its signal is never passed to apiRequest, so `cancel` does not abort the request. (3) `execute` clears pendingConfig on success, so `retryFailed` (which requires pendingConfig) effectively returns null unless confirm is called again. (4) The parser requires success+failed to equal the requested count, which seems incompatible with an asynchronous job response that is still in progress. (5) The async setInterval callback can overlap requests. (6) Simulated progress is cosmetic.

Pass abortController.signal to the request and handle abort. Keep the last config so retryFailed works after execute. Add interval cleanup on unmount and a guard against overlapping executes.

Several behaviours look incomplete or buggy. (1) The AbortController is created but never passed to apiRequest, so cancel() cannot abort the in-flight request. (2) pollJobProgress only starts a setInterval and returns immediately, so `await pollJobProgress` does not wait for the job. In job mode, toasts, onSuccess and invalidateQueries are never run, and result is not updated with the final job outcome. (3) execute clears pendingConfig on success, so retryFailed (which needs pendingConfig) returns null after a normal run. pendingConfig is only set by confirm(). (4) No unmount cleanup of the intervals. (5) onProgress is called inside a setState updater, which is a side effect. (6) The ETA division can produce Infinity when elapsed is 0. (7) onSuccess is not called in the all-failed case, and onError is not called either.
